l: Dionysius's military preparation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius's military preparation organized craftsmen from his dominions, Italy, and Greece to produce weapons and ships, built harbor facilities, and recruited soldiers from Sicily, Greece, and especially Lacedaemon. It produced extensive arms, artillery, and warships, including five-oared galleys, before assembling about eighty thousand infantry and over three thousand cavalry.

l: Dionysius's speech for war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: advocates_war_against Carthaginians [on behalf of the Syracusans] Dionysius told the Syracusans that the Carthaginians were implacable enemies of the Grecians and were continually plotting to ruin the Sicilians. He argued that they should be attacked while weakened by the plague rather than after they had recovered their strength.

l: Carthaginian enslavement of Greek cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius accused the Carthaginians of having subdued Greek cities and depriving them of their laws and liberties. He used this grievance to demand their restoration and to persuade the Syracusans and other Greeks to support the war.

l: Himiico, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himiico, a Carthaginian general, sails from Carthage with one hundred galleys to surprise Dionysius’s fleet at Motya, destroys and burns ships, then returns to Africa after abandoning the attack against stronger defenses and forces.

l: Motyans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Motyans resisted Dionysius's army with weapons, firebrands, and hand-to-hand fighting from their walls, buildings, and rooftops. After their defenses were breached and the city was captured, many were killed, while those who survived were sold as slaves.

l: Himiico's naval attack on Motya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himiico's naval attack on Motya was a surprise sea assault on the Syracusan fleet in Motya's harbour, destroying and burning ships before failing as land-based missile fire protected the remainder and Dionysius moved it out by land.

l: capture of Motya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_carried_out_by Dionysius's army [after breaking into the city] Dionysius's army captured Motya after overcoming its determined defenders. The city was then ravaged by the Sicilians, who killed many inhabitants and carried away silver, gold, rich garments, and other treasure.

l: Dionysius's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A Syracusan army used six-floored siege towers and rams, advanced at night through Motya's breach and buildings, then captured the city amid killing and plunder.

l: the Syracusan fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Syracusan fleet, stationed in Motya’s harbor, was trapped when Himiico seized the passage. Dionysius had it dragged overland to sea, where it escaped, fought pursuing Carthaginians, captured their admiral, destroyed twenty ships, and later aided Dionysius’s harbor attack.

l: Mago, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mago is a Carthaginian general in Sicily who commands Carthaginians and eighty thousand soldiers. He seeks to restore Carthaginian affairs through mild treatment, alliances, and opposition to Dionysius, suffers defeat near Abacene, later leads an invasion causing defections, then leaves after peace.

l: destruction of Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himilco ordered Messana to be pulled down and burned after capturing it. The houses were destroyed so completely that the formerly inhabited city could scarcely be identified.

l: naval battle of Catana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_participant Dionysius [through Leptinus and the Sicilian fleet] At Catana, Leptinus led the Sicilian fleet against Mago's Carthaginian fleet. Leptinus's advance force was surrounded, the Sicilian fleet was routed after he fled, more than one hundred Sicilian vessels were sunk or captured, and more than twenty thousand men were killed.

l: siege of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himilco brought his army and fleet to Syracuse, challenged the Syracusans to battle, ravaged the surrounding country, and established forts near the sea to support a long blockade. The Syracusans defended the city, and their skirmishes sometimes defeated or frightened the Carthaginians.

l: plague among the Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A disease seized the Carthaginians after they began operations against Syracuse. As their fortunes reversed following earlier successes in Sicily and defeat by sea and land, the plague killed one hundred and fifty thousand men, leaving their bodies unburied on the ground.

l: Leptines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Leptines, brother and fleet commander of Dionysius, aided the Lucanians, rescued about a thousand Greek swimmers and secured their ransom, then made peace with Italians; Dionysius dismissed him because it hindered his plans.

l: Theodorus's speech, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Theodorus's speech called for Dionysius to abdicate and leave Syracuse with his possessions, or for the armed Syracusans and their allies to seize their liberty. It portrayed Dionysius as a tyrant who had ruined cities, robbed temples, oppressed citizens, and repeatedly failed against the Carthaginians.

l: the assembly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius called the assembly after the Syracusans' naval success and praised their courage. The assembly heard Theodorus's attack on Dionysius, but Pharacides rejected the call to remove him; Dionysius then dissolved the assembly.

l: the naval victory at Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_won_by the Syracusans [against the Carthaginian fleet] The naval victory began when Syracusans captured a provision ship and were pursued by forty Carthaginian ships. The Syracusans took the admiral, destroyed twenty ships, drove off the rest, and brought their captured vessels into the city.

l: the surprise attack on the Carthaginian camp and fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius assembled the army at night and reached the Carthaginian camp near daybreak without being discovered. The attack captured the castle called Polictima and a fort near Dascon, while the fleet assaulted the anchored Carthaginian ships and threw them into confusion.

l: the burning of the Carthaginian ships, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: destroys the Carthaginian ships [including transports and ships at anchor] The Syracusans set fire to forty Carthaginian ships of fifty oars each, along with transport ships and other vessels near Dascon. Wind and broken cables spread the flames, causing ships to collide, burn, break apart, or scatter until all were destroyed.

l: Syracusan liberty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_opposed_by Dionysius's tyranny [the stated political conflict] Syracusan liberty was the central objective of Theodorus's appeal. He argued that the citizens were armed and supported by allies, giving them an opportunity to depose Dionysius and restore their laws.

l: Dionysius's tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius's tyranny ruled Syracuse through mercenaries, slaves, and a fortified castle, stripping laws and liberty while imposing executions, banishments, confiscations, forced marriages, sacrilege, enslavement, and Sicilian cities' destruction or abandonment.

l: rebels, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rebels in Africa, aided by slaves, assembled free people and slaves into an army reportedly of two hundred thousand, captured Tunis and defeated Carthaginians near Carthage. Lacking officers and provisions, divided over command, and weakened by bribery and desertion, they dispersed.

l: Abacene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Abacene was a city of Mago's confederates and the site of his camp after his campaign near Messana. Dionysius attacked him there and defeated the Carthaginians.

l: Carthaginian defeat at Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Carthaginian defeat at Syracuse involved simultaneous reverses by sea and land. Dionysius’s forces destroyed much of the Carthaginian fleet, captured or dispersed the army, and forced the Carthaginians to abandon their Sicilian allies and retreat toward Africa.

l: African revolt against Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a revolt [by Carthage's African confederates] The African revolt against Carthage began when Carthage’s confederates, angered by its abandonment of the soldiers at Syracuse and encouraged by its misfortune, sought their liberty. The rebels captured Tunis and defeated the Carthaginians, but their army later dissolved because of shortages, internal quarrels, bribery, treachery, and desertion.

l: Agesilaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Agesilaus is one of the two Lacedaemonian kings and a military general. Sent from Europe to Ephesus, he enlarged his army, campaigned in Asia, defeated Tissaphernes's forces, and made a truce with Tithraustes. Recalled, he marched through Macedonia and Thessaly into Boeotia, won at Coronea, and was severely wounded and taken to Delphos.

l: Persian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war [between the Lacedaemonians and Persians] The Lacedaemonians anticipated a great war with the Persians and organized an expedition under Agesilaus. The conflict included campaigning in Asia, naval operations around Caunus and Rhodes, and Persian support for Conon's effort against the Lacedaemonian fleet.

l: Caunus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a castle [in Caria] Caunus was besieged by Pharax, who had arrived there with the Lacedaemonian fleet. The siege ended when Artaphemes and Pharnabazus came to its relief.

l: Agesilaus's campaign in Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a military campaign [conducted in Asia] Agesilaus's campaign took him from Ephesus through the Caystrian plains, Mysia, the region near Sipylus, and toward Sardis. His army plundered Persian possessions, defeated Tissaphernes's forces, and later returned to the sea because the sacrifices did not indicate great success farther inland.

l: Sipylus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a rising ground [occupied by Agesilaus] Sipylus was where Agesilaus occupied the rising ground with a phalanx and defeated the forces of Tissaphernes. The Lacedaemonians killed six thousand Persians in the pursuit and captured many prisoners and a rich camp.

l: Battle of Sipylus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [victory of the Lacedaemonians over Tissaphernes] In the battle near Sipylus, Agesilaus used an ambush and wheeled his army against the Persians attacking his rear. The Persians fled after being surrounded; six thousand were killed, many were taken prisoner, and the Lacedaemonians seized their rich camp.

l: Parysatis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a queen-mother [mother of Artaxerxes] Parysatis, the queen-mother, urged Artaxerxes on her knees to take revenge on Tissaphernes. She hated him because he had helped frustrate her son's expedition against his brother.

l: execution of Tissaphernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a execution [carried out at Colosse in Phrygia] Tissaphernes was seized by Tithraustes in a bath at Colosse in Phrygia. His head was cut off and sent to Artaxerxes.

l: Haliartus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city [besieged by Lysander and the Phocians] Haliartus was besieged by Lysander and the Phocians. The Boeotians and Athenians came to its aid, and a battle there resulted in Lysander's death and the defeat of the Lacedaemonians.

l: Battle of Haliartus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [between the Lacedaemonians and the Boeotians with Athenian allies] At the Battle of Haliartus, the Boeotians and Athenians defeated Lysander, many Lacedaemonians, and their confederates. The Boeotians lost two hundred Thebans through falls from steep precipices.

l: Conon's mission to Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Conon went to Artaxerxes at Babylon and promised to ruin the Lacedaemonian fleet if supplied with money and other necessities. Artaxerxes rewarded him, appointed a paymaster, and allowed him to choose a Persian colleague, whom Conon chose as Pharnabazus.

l: Persian navy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a navy [commanded by Conon] The Persian naval forces included Conon's fleet, which numbered forty ships at Caunus and later eighty galleys at Chersonesus. Conon also received ten ships from Cilicia and eighty from Phoenicia.

l: Marcus Furius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Marcus Furius, made dictator during a Volscian attack, marches by night to destroy the Volsci from behind, then defeats the Aequi and Gauls.

l: general assembly at Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A Corinthian general assembly united several cities' representatives, arranged war matters, and sent messengers that won further defections from the Lacedaemonians.

l: Aricas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city of Locris [said to be the birthplace of Ajax] Aricas was identified as a city of Locris and the supposed birthplace of Ajax. It was the site of a battle between the Boeotians and the Phocians.

l: battle at Aricas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [won by the Boeotians] The battle at Aricas was a sharp engagement between the Boeotians and Phocians. The Boeotians won, killed more than one thousand of the enemy, and lost five hundred of their own.

l: river Nemea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The river Nemea was the site of a battle between the Lacedaemonians and their confederates and the Boeotians and their confederates.

l: battle of Nemea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [ended when night parted the armies] The battle of Nemea continued until night separated the armies, with both sides prevailing in different parts of the field. The Lacedaemonians and their confederates lost eleven hundred, while the Boeotians and their confederates lost two thousand eight hundred.

l: Pisander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Lacedaemonian admiral Pisander is identified in the heading as the Lacedaemonian admiral defeated at Cnidus. A note in the text states that the name Periarchus is mistaken there for Pisander.

l: battle of Cnidus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a sea battle [between the Lacedaemonian and Persian fleets] At the battle of Cnidus, the Persian fleet defeated the Lacedaemonian fleet after the Lacedaemonian confederates fled. The Lacedaemonians lost fifty ships and five hundred prisoners, and afterward lost their sovereignty of the sea.

l: Corinthian sedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: In Corinth, conspirators seeking power began an eight-year sedition, killing 120 citizens and banishing 500 with Argive aid, provoking Lacedaemonian intervention and fighting.

l: Iphicrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Athenian commander [at Corinth] Iphicrates commanded forces defending the Corinthian faction and defeated the exiles near the Lechaeum. He also defeated Lacedaemonians near Corinth and fought successfully at Phlius and Sicyon before giving up his intended control of Corinthian territory.

l: Heloris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A Syracusan made general of Italian Greek forces, he opposed Dionysius after banishment, advanced toward Caulonia, and was killed with nearly all accompanying troops.

l: battle of Abacene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [won by Dionysius against the Carthaginians] At the battle of Abacene, Dionysius attacked Mago's army after it had returned from ravaging the country near Messana. The Carthaginians were routed and lost more than eight hundred men.

l: Lucanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lucanians made an incursion into the territories of the Thurians and later defeated the Thurians after surrounding them in a plain. They killed more than ten thousand Italians, accepted ransoms for survivors rescued by Leptines, and made peace with the Italians.

l: Greek confederacy against Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a confederacy [formed by Boeotians, Athenians, Corinthians, Argives and other Greek communities] The Greek confederacy against Sparta included the Boeotians, Athenians, Corinthians, and Argives, and attracted Euboea, the Leucadians, Acarnanians, Ambracians, and Chalcidonians of Thrace. It was formed to overcome Lacedaemonian power and oppose its tyrannical government.

l: Spartan tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a tyrannical government [imposed by the Lacedaemonians on their confederates] The Lacedaemonians' tyrannical government caused their confederates to hate them. This hostility encouraged cities to leave the Lacedaemonian side and join the opposing confederacy.

l: rebuilding of the Athenian walls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_led_by Conon [with Persian support] Conon promised to rebuild the walls of Athens and the long walls of the Piraeus, which the Lacedaemonians had demolished after the Peloponnesian War. He hired workers and used men from his fleet, while the Thebans and other cities supplied additional assistance.

l: sea power of Lacedaemon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_lost_by Lacedaemonians [after the revolts of the Asian cities] Lacedaemonian sea power was broken after the battle of Cnidus. As cities revolted and accepted Conon's protection, the Lacedaemonians lost sovereignty of the sea.

l: Struthius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Persian general [against the Lacedaemonians] Artaxerxes appointed Struthius as general and sent him against the Lacedaemonians on the sea-coasts. Struthius commanded a large force, including cavalry, heavy-armed troops, and light-armed troops, and defeated Thimbron by surprise.

l: war in Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Carthaginians renewed the war in Sicily under Mago and initially caused several Sicilian cities to defect from Dionysius. Dionysius isolated the Carthaginian army through Agyrus and local attacks on its supplies, after which the war ended in a negotiated peace.

l: peace between Carthage and Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a peace treaty [settles the war in Sicily] Dionysius concluded peace with the Carthaginians after their ambassadors sought terms. The agreement required the Sicilians to be subject to Dionysius and granted him Taurominium.

l: Rhodes' defection from Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a political defection [Rhodes sided with the Lacedaemonians] Rhodes defected from Athens, expelled the citizens who favored Athens, and defeated those who took up arms to defend the Athenian interest. Lacedaemonian forces then assisted in arranging affairs in the city, while Rhodian exiles later resisted the city from a castle.

l: Evagoras' war against Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war [Evagoras against Persian authority in Cyprus] Evagoras's expansion from Salamis brought him into conflict with Persia after rival Cypriot cities appealed to Artaxerxes. Artaxerxes ordered naval preparations and directed Hecatomnus to make war against Evagoras.

l: Thimbron's campaign in Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Lacedaemonian military campaign [against Struthius and Persia] Thimbron's campaign was directed against Struthius and Persian territory in Asia. He occupied Jonda and Corossus and ravaged the king's provinces, but Struthius later surprised and killed him.

l: Caulonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Caulonia was besieged by Dionysius and later captured after the defeat of the Italian forces. Dionysius transported its inhabitants to Syracuse, razed the city, and gave its territory to the Locrians.

l: war between the Lucanians and the Thurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war began when the Lucanians invaded Thurian territory. The Thurians advanced without waiting for their allies, were trapped and decisively defeated in Lucania, and saw many survivors rescued by Leptines. Leptines's intervention helped bring the Lucanians and Italians to peace.

l: Dionysius's expedition against Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius first attacked the territory of Rhegium with an army and fleet, but Rhegian forces helped defeat his naval assault and he narrowly escaped drowning. In a later expedition, he secured Rhegium's fleet and hostages through an agreement, then used a dispute over provisions as a pretext to break the league and besiege the city.

l: siege of Caulonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius transported his forces to Caulonia and closely besieged the city with engines. After defeating the Italian relief army at the river Helorus, he removed the inhabitants to Syracuse and razed Caulonia to the ground.

l: battle at the river Helorus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: At the river Helorus, Dionysius attacked Heloris and five hundred leading troops before the rest of the Italian army could form. Heloris and almost all his party were killed, the Italian Greeks were routed, and more than ten thousand survivors eventually surrendered after being deprived of water.

l: siege of Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The siege of Rhegium lasted eleven months as Dionysius attacked daily; Philo’s defenders made sorties and burned engines, but famine ultimately forced surrender, with many inhabitants captured or enslaved.

l: Antalcidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a admiral [of the Lacedaemonians] Antalcidas was sent by the Lacedaemonians to Artaxerxes to arrange peace. He delivered the Lacedaemonians' embassy and obtained terms that ended their war.

l: Euagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Euagoras, ruler of Cyprus, raises a large army during Artaxerxes’s war with the Greeks, prompting Artaxerxes to prepare war against him.

l: Philo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a governor [of Rhegium] Philo, the governor of Rhegium, was bound in chains after the city's surrender. Dionysius had Philo's son drowned, subjected Philo to public humiliation and torture, and finally ordered him and his kindred to be drowned.

l: Allia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a river [four-score furlongs from Rome] The river Allia was the site of a major Roman defeat by the Gauls. The Roman army was routed there, and many Romans were killed or drowned while fleeing toward the river.

l: Capitol, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a fortified stronghold [where the Romans took refuge during the Gallic occupation] The Romans brought food, valuables, and other possessions into the Capitol and defended it against the Gauls. The Gauls besieged it and attempted to climb its rock, but their attack was discovered when the sacred geese raised an alarm.

l: Pontius Camillus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Roman messenger [who entered the Capitol from Veii] Pontius Camillus secretly crossed the Tiber by night and climbed the Capitol's steep rock to inform the besieged Romans that the forces at Veii intended to attack the Gauls. He then returned to Veii by the same route.

l: Peace of Antalcidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a peace treaty [between Artaxerxes and the Grecians] The Peace of Antalcidas ended the war between the Lacedaemonians and the Grecians on terms set by Artaxerxes. The Greek cities in Asia were to return to obedience, while the other Grecians were to govern their own cities according to their laws.

l: Gallic invasion of Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Gauls crossed the Alps in a large army and occupied territory between the Apennines and the Alps. They drove out the Tyrrhenians, fought at Clusium, and marched toward Rome after the Roman ambassadors' dispute with them.

l: Battle of the Allia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [between the Romans and the Gauls] At the Battle of the Allia, the Gauls routed the Roman army after defeating the Roman troops positioned on the hills and disordering the rest. Many Romans were killed on the field, at the riverbank, or while attempting to swim across the Tiber.

l: sack of Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Gauls entered Rome after the Roman defeat and destroyed the city, sparing only a few houses on Mount Palatine. They continued to besiege the Romans who held the Capitol until peace was arranged for a payment of gold.

l: Volscian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Volscian revolt began after the Romans had been impoverished and weakened by the Gallic calamity. The Volsci attacked the Roman camp but were defeated and nearly annihilated by Marcus Furius.

l: Roman victory over the Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Romans later recovered from the Gallic attack and fought the Gauls under Marcus Furius. Marcus Furius defeated them near Sutrium or on their march from Rome, recovered much of their plunder, and seized the gold taken at Rome.

l: famine at Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The famine at Rhegium became so severe that the inhabitants ate horses, beasts of burden, boiled skins, leather, and grass. Dionysius worsened their misery by allowing his own carriage horses and draught animals to consume the remaining grass, forcing Rhegium to surrender.

Him the omnipotent Father, taking up among encircling clouds, bears aloft amid the glittering stars, in his chariot drawn by {its} four steeds.

s: Deïanira receives tunic of Nessus (as a supposed love charm)
q: Nessus takes it out, and says to himself, “And yet I shall not die unrevenged;” and gives his garment, dyed in the warm blood, as a present to her whom he is carrying off, as though an incentive to love.

s: Deïanira sends tunic of Nessus (to restore Hercules's declining love)
q: Before them all, she prefers to send the garment dyed in the blood of Nessus, to restore strength to his declining love.

q: Whither, thou ravisher, does thy vain confidence in thy feet hurry thee? to thee am I speaking, Nessus, thou two-shaped {monster}.

s: Nessus attempts abduction of Deïanira (while carrying her across Evenus)
q: he recognizes the voice of his wife; and as Nessus is preparing to rob him of what he has entrusted to his care
